title: Pygmalion Goes to Boot Camp
text:
In the early 1980s the organizational psychologist Dov Eden and his colleague Abraham Shani ran a field experiment in an Israel Defense Forces combat command course. Trainees were going through a fifteen week program, and four instructors were responsible for them.

Before the course began, the instructors were told that, based on test scores, ratings from earlier courses and evaluations, each trainee had been rated as having high, regular or unknown command potential. In fact the labels had been assigned at random. The trainees themselves were not told.

At the end of the course, the trainees labeled as high potential scored clearly higher on objective achievement tests in subjects such as combat tactics and navigation. They also reported more positive attitudes toward the course and a stronger wish to go on to further training. Their ratings of their instructors showed why: the instructors had, without realizing it, led them differently.

Eden and Shani concluded that a leader's expectations alone could change how much people learned and achieved. Eden spent much of his later career showing similar effects in other workplaces.
lesson: People tend to rise or sink to what their leader expects of them. Show genuine belief in your team's ability, and back it with real support and challenge.
location: Israel Defense Forces training base, Israel
source: Eden, D., and Shani, A. B. (1982). Pygmalion goes to boot camp: Expectancy, leadership, and trainee performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 67(2), 194-199.
